title: Fast Changes, and the Road to Memory

scenes.tts: Some changes last milliseconds, not hours. Do they follow the same rule?
scenes.visual: Two time axes: one in hours, one in milliseconds.
scenes.narration: Some changes last milliseconds, not hours. Do they follow the same rule?

scenes.tts: No. The facilitation and depression shown here are a different machine. They need no postsynaptic coincidence, and they work mainly in the presynaptic terminal. Short term plasticity also includes other mechanisms.
scenes.caption: No. The facilitation and depression shown here are a different machine. They need no postsynaptic coincidence, and they work mainly in the presynaptic terminal. Short-term plasticity also includes other mechanisms.
scenes.visual: The view shifts from the spine to the presynaptic terminal, full of vesicles.
scenes.narration: No. The facilitation and depression shown here are a different machine. They need no postsynaptic coincidence, and they work mainly in the presynaptic terminal. Short-term plasticity also includes other mechanisms.

scenes.tts: Give two pulses close together. Divide the second response by the first. That is the paired pulse ratio.
scenes.caption: Give two pulses close together. Divide the second response by the first. That is the paired-pulse ratio.
scenes.visual: Two stimulus ticks and two responses; the second is divided by the first on screen.
scenes.narration: Give two pulses close together. Divide the second response by the first. That is the paired-pulse ratio.

scenes.tts: Above one is facilitation. Below one is depression.
scenes.visual: Left: second response larger, labelled facilitation. Right: second response smaller, labelled depression.
scenes.narration: Above one is facilitation. Below one is depression.

scenes.tts: The classic explanation for facilitation is residual calcium, left in the terminal from the first spike.
scenes.visual: Ca2+ dots linger in the terminal after the first spike and add to the second.
scenes.narration: The classic explanation for facilitation is residual calcium, left in the terminal from the first spike.

scenes.tts: In 2016, Jackman, Regehr and colleagues deleted synaptotagmin 7 in mice. Facilitation was lost at the synapses tested, though residual calcium was unchanged.
scenes.visual: Caption card: Jackman, Regehr and colleagues, 2016. Residual Ca2+ is the same, but the second response no longer grows.
scenes.narration: In 2016, Jackman, Regehr and colleagues deleted synaptotagmin 7 in mice. Facilitation was lost at the synapses tested, though residual calcium was unchanged.

scenes.tts: So at those synapses, synaptotagmin 7 is a sensor that reads the leftover calcium.
scenes.visual: A sensor icon labelled synaptotagmin 7 lights up when the leftover Ca2+ touches it.
scenes.narration: So at those synapses, synaptotagmin 7 is a sensor that reads the leftover calcium.

scenes.tts: Depression has a simple candidate. The first spike uses up vesicles.
scenes.visual: The first pulse releases a share of the vesicle pool; fewer remain.
scenes.narration: Depression has a simple candidate. The first spike uses up vesicles.

scenes.tts: In a simple depletion model, with no refilling and no facilitation, the first pulse releases 40 percent of the pool. Will the second response be larger or smaller?
scenes.caption: In a simple depletion model, with no refilling and no facilitation, the first pulse releases 40% of the pool. Will the second response be larger or smaller?
scenes.visual: On screen: F = 0.40; no refilling, no facilitation, same F on both pulses, same current per vesicle. A question mark over the second response.
scenes.narration: In a simple depletion model, with no refilling and no facilitation, the first pulse releases 40% of the pool. Will the second response be larger or smaller?

scenes.tts: Smaller. Sixty percent of the pool is left, so the second response is 60 percent of the first.
scenes.caption: Smaller. 60% of the pool is left, so the second response is 60% of the first.
scenes.visual: The pool shrinks to 60%. On screen: ratio = 1 − F = 0.60.
scenes.narration: Smaller. 60% of the pool is left, so the second response is 60% of the first.

scenes.tts: But a ratio like that does not prove depletion. Other processes can give the same number.
scenes.visual: A caution card: a ratio of 0.60 does not prove depletion.
scenes.narration: But a ratio like that does not prove depletion. Other processes can give the same number.

scenes.tts: Now back to Hebb. Does memory actually use L T P?
scenes.caption: Now back to Hebb. Does memory actually use LTP?
scenes.visual: The Hebb card from chapter 1 returns, with a brain outline behind it.
scenes.narration: Now back to Hebb. Does memory actually use LTP?

scenes.tts: A correlation, learning alongside potentiation, is not proof.
scenes.visual: A ladder with three rungs: correlation, necessity, sufficiency. The lowest rung lights.
scenes.narration: A correlation, learning alongside potentiation, is not proof.

scenes.tts: In 1986, Morris and colleagues infused an N M D A blocker into rats. Place learning was impaired, a visual task was spared, and hippocampal L T P was suppressed.
scenes.caption: In 1986, Morris and colleagues infused an NMDA blocker into rats. Place learning was impaired, a visual task was spared, and hippocampal LTP was suppressed.
scenes.visual: Caption card: Morris and colleagues, 1986, AP5. A rat in a water maze; a visual task is learned normally; an LTP plot stays flat.
scenes.narration: In 1986, Morris and colleagues infused an NMDA blocker into rats. Place learning was impaired, a visual task was spared, and hippocampal LTP was suppressed.

scenes.tts: But the drug reached many synapses. It showed the receptors were needed for both, not that the learning was L T P.
scenes.caption: But the drug reached many synapses. It showed the receptors were needed for both, not that the learning was LTP.
scenes.visual: The necessity rung lights, with a caveat tag.
scenes.narration: But the drug reached many synapses. It showed the receptors were needed for both, not that the learning was LTP.

scenes.tts: In 2014, Nabavi, Malinow and colleagues used light on auditory inputs to the rat lateral amygdala, as a cue.
scenes.visual: Caption card: Nabavi, Malinow and colleagues, 2014. Light-gated inputs to the lateral amygdala glow.
scenes.narration: In 2014, Nabavi, Malinow and colleagues used light on auditory inputs to the rat lateral amygdala, as a cue.

scenes.tts: After light was paired with shock, the light suppressed lever pressing. Optical L T D of those inputs removed the response.
scenes.caption: After light was paired with shock, the light suppressed lever pressing. Optical LTD of those inputs removed the response.
scenes.visual: A rat stops pressing a lever when the light comes on; after optical LTD, it presses again.
scenes.narration: After light was paired with shock, the light suppressed lever pressing. Optical LTD of those inputs removed the response.

scenes.tts: Optical L T P afterwards restored it.
scenes.caption: Optical LTP afterwards restored it.
scenes.visual: After optical LTP, the light suppresses pressing again.
scenes.narration: Optical LTP afterwards restored it.

scenes.tts: Is L T P at these inputs enough, on its own, to create the memory?
scenes.caption: Is LTP at these inputs enough, on its own, to create the memory?
scenes.visual: The sufficiency rung with a question mark.
scenes.narration: Is LTP at these inputs enough, on its own, to create the memory?

scenes.tts: No. In rats never given the pairing, L T P at these inputs produced no response. Something set up by the pairing had to be there. That holds for this pathway, in rats, in this task.
scenes.caption: No. In rats never given the pairing, LTP at these inputs produced no response. Something set up by the pairing had to be there. That holds for this pathway, in rats, in this task.
scenes.visual: An unpaired rat given optical LTP keeps pressing the lever.
scenes.narration: No. In rats never given the pairing, LTP at these inputs produced no response. Something set up by the pairing had to be there. That holds for this pathway, in rats, in this task.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: fast changes are mostly a separate, presynaptic machine. And linking L T P to memory takes tests of necessity and sufficiency, not correlation alone.
scenes.caption: The takeaway: fast changes are mostly a separate, presynaptic machine. And linking LTP to memory takes tests of necessity and sufficiency, not correlation alone.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: the short-term examples here are mainly presynaptic, with no pre-post coincidence; linking LTP to memory needs necessity and sufficiency tests, with scope stated.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: fast changes are mostly a separate, presynaptic machine. And linking LTP to memory takes tests of necessity and sufficiency, not correlation alone.
